units: the narrator writes to an acquaintance who had asked for news of him
he was taken on by an elderly cabinetmaker looking for a beginner
the master handed him a tool and a piece of wood without any explanation
his first week went entirely on a single cutting movement
the sign of success was a shaving coming off unbroken
he was then allowed to smooth the surfaces the master had prepared
his first box was judged clumsy but honest
he now draws his own designs at home in the evening
he concludes that patience is learnt through practice and not through talk
he invites his correspondent to come and see the workshop
text: You asked how the workshop was treating me, and I have put off answering long enough. When the leaves turned, I walked into a narrow shop where an elderly cabinetmaker wanted a beginner. He handed me a plane and a rough board, and said nothing at all about what I should do with them. For a whole week I did one thing: push that plane, over and over, until the shaving came away in a single unbroken ribbon. Once the cold set in, he let me smooth the surfaces he had roughed out himself. By the thaw I had made my first small box, which he called clumsy but honest. Now I draw my own designs in the evening, at the kitchen table. What I have learnt here will not fit into a letter: patience comes through the hands, never through talk. Write back soon, and tell me whether you will come and see the workshop.

units: the bubbles in a casting come from filling the mould too fast
the trapped air leaves hollows that weaken the piece
pouring very slowly is not the answer
an alloy that loses its heat too early fails to fill the whole cavity
heating the mould beforehand holds off the hardening of the metal
this preheating removes the need to pour more slowly
bubbles that persist point to air escaping badly
the craftsman cuts thin channels to let the air out as the metal rises
surface flaws come back either to heat or to the path taken by the air
text: Why does a casting come out of the mould with bubbles across its face? Look first at how fast it was filled: metal poured in a rush traps air, and that trapped air leaves hollows which weaken the piece. Should the pour then be as slow as the hand can manage? No. An alloy that loses its heat on the way in stiffens before it has reached every corner of the cavity, and the shape comes out short. What does the founder rely on instead? He heats the mould before pouring, which holds off solidification without forcing him to slow the stream. And if bubbles show up all the same? Then the air is not getting out. The moulder cuts vents, thin channels that let it escape as the metal level climbs. Every blemish on the surface leads back either to heat or to the path the air had to take.

units: a visitor reports that her old book is shedding its leaves
she fears the volume will come apart completely
the specialist puts the fault down to broken sewing
the original adhesive has grown crumbly and no longer holds
he dismisses the idea of giving up on the repair
putting it right means taking the gatherings apart one by one
the old adhesive comes away with moisture
the old outside will be kept and strengthened from within
how long it takes depends on drying under a press that cannot be hurried
text: The visitor told the bookbinder that her old family volume was shedding its leaves, and that she feared the whole thing would come apart. He answered that the original sewing had snapped and that the glue, gone crumbly, no longer held anything together. She asked whether the repair was worth attempting. He assured her that it was, then set out what it involved: taking the gatherings apart one by one, lifting the old glue with moisture, and sewing afresh onto tapes. She wondered how it would look afterwards. The binder explained that the old covering would stay where it was, with a fresh lining set inside the boards, so that the work would hardly show. She asked how long it would take. He said that drying under the press kept its own pace and that nothing could hurry it. She accepted, reassured by his plainness.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old building sites knew two ways of organising stone cutting
under the first, one worker took a block from start to finish
under the second, the stages were shared out between specialised groups
the individual arrangement gave very even pieces
it moved at a slow pace and depended on the skill available
the shared arrangement raised output
it made learning easier by isolating a single movement
it called for strict checking of the way the pieces came together
the two methods leave distinct material clues
those clues inform researchers where no written documents exist
text: Old building sites cut their stone in one of two ways. Under the first, a single mason took a block from start to finish, squaring it, dressing it and carving the detail. Under the second, each stage passed to a team that did nothing else. Work done by one pair of hands came out remarkably even, since the same judgement governed every proportion, but it moved slowly and hung on whatever skill happened to be at hand. Splitting the stages raised output, and it brought learners on faster, since each had only one movement to master. The price was strict checking as the blocks came together, or nothing would sit true. Each method left its own marks in the stone: even tool traces on the one side, scored setting-out lines on the other. Where no records survive, that is what scholars read.

units: a pottery workshop holds three families of implements
the first family serves to give the shape
flat blades bring the wall upright while it is being shaped
the second family serves to take material away
thin metal loops lighten the underside of the pot
the third family gathers the tools of the final stage
points serve to decorate or to mark the pot
beginners overrate the part played by the turning machine
a badly smoothed wall takes up the glazed coating poorly
success rests on the order of the stages more than on nimble fingers
text: Walk into a pottery workshop and you will soon find yourself sorting the tools into three families. First come the ones that give the shape: the wheel, obviously, but also ribs, those flat blades you hold against the wall of the pot to bring it upright. Then come the ones that take clay away: loop tools, thin metal loops that pare off the surplus weight under the foot. Last comes everything to do with finishing, sponges, cloths, soft brushes, and the fine points for marking or decorating a pot. Beginners tend to believe that the wheel does the work. It does not. A wall left rough will drink the glaze unevenly, and the pot suffers for it. Each family picks up what the one before it missed, and it is that order of steps, far more than clever fingers, which decides how a piece turns out.

units: the workshop in the hamlet had closed when the man running it left
a woman metalworker bought it two winters later for a small sum
she began by clearing the rubble out of the building
she found the old ventilation device in good order
a former pupil of the place came to explain how the tools were stored
the hearth was put back into service at the start of the warm season
she now makes fastenings to order
she trains two apprentices every season
she finds it harder to convince customers that handwork lasts
text: The forge in the hamlet had gone cold when its last master left. Two winters on, a welder from the next valley bought the building for almost nothing, without much faith at first in what she was taking on. She began by clearing the rubble out of the shed, and under a tarpaulin she came across the original bellows, still sound. An old apprentice of the place, told by a neighbour that someone had moved in, walked over to show her where the tongs and the swages had always been kept. The hearth was lit again as the mild weather came round. Since then she has been forging locks and hinges to order, and takes on two trainees a season. Hammering iron, she says, was never the hard part. Convincing customers that a fitting shaped by hand outlasts one stamped out by a press is another matter.

units: the leather must be softened with a greasy product before assembly
a dried-out hide splits under pressure and cannot be mended
the holes are punched in one movement with the blade held straight
a slanted hole tips the metal fastening
the head of the fastening is struck with short repeated blows
a single heavy blow deforms the seat of the fastening
the lining inside must not form any fold
a fold makes the assembly sink under use
the rim of the head is smoothed to remove the tool marks
a sharp edge ends up cutting the thread that touches it
text: Before you set a single rivet, oil the leather and let it drink right through. Dry hide splits under pressure, and a split never closes again. Punch your holes in one clean stroke with the awl held true, since a hole driven at a slant tips the rivet, and the collar then bites crooked. Slide the shank home, cap it with its washer, and work the head with short taps rather than heavy blows. One hard strike flattens the metal sideways and spoils the seat it ought to sit in. Check at every stage that the lining inside has not rucked up, because a fold will let the whole assembly sink under use and the stitching will give way in the middle. Last of all, take your time smoothing the rim of the head, so that no tool marks remain: a sharp edge will cut through any thread that brushes it.

units: glass-blowing workshops share the same burden over energy
their furnaces have to be kept hot without a break
a mass of glass that has cooled cracks when the heat comes back
the workshops keep firing even when orders fall away
that obligation weighs heavily on what they spend
several workshops are trying out a shared furnace kept alight at all times
the blowers come to draw their material at slots spread through the day
the system calls for containers that can be moved and better insulation
the first readings show less fuel burnt for each object made
the arrangement does not suit workshops too far from the shared furnace
text: In a valley where glass has been blown for generations, the workshops all live with the same burden: their furnaces can never be allowed to cool down, since a chilled mass of glass cracks the moment the heat comes back into it. So the makers keep the fire up even when orders thin out, and the bill for that weighs heavily on what they spend. A group of workshops has just tried out a shared answer. One furnace, held at heat around the clock, serves the blowers of the neighbourhood in turn, each of them coming to draw glass at an agreed slot. It calls for pots that can be shifted, insulation of a better sort, and a firm hold on the timetable. The first readings show less fuel burnt for each object made. Those running it accept that the arrangement suits nobody sited too far from the shared furnace.

units: two hammers lying together look identical at first glance
the metal-beater's hammer has a rounded polished head
that head leaves no mark on the surface it strikes
its handle is short and thick, for a quick movement
the decorator's tool has a light, almost flat head
its handle thins down and turns supple towards the grip
the first tool shifts the material in bulk
the second works only on the surface
the traces of wear differ sharply from one tool to the other
neither can stand in for the other
text: Two hammers lie next to each other on the workbench, and a careless glance would readily take them for one and the same tool. The first belongs to the metal-beater: its head is domed and polished, so that it slides over the sheet without printing any mark on it, and the handle is short and thick, cut for a quick stroke. The second is the chaser's. Its head is light, almost flat, and the shaft narrows steadily towards the grip until it flexes under the fingers. The one drives the metal into shape, the other barely grazes it. Wear tells the same story: the beater's cheeks are scuffed all over, while the edges of the chaser's head stay crisp. Set together, they speak of two opposite dealings with matter, the one after volume, the other after the mark. Neither could ever stand in for the other.

units: teaching often ranks the manual trades as a fallback
that ranking misses the mental demand of skilled movement
fine adjustment calls for constant judgement of the material
no written work replaces that direct reading
repeating a movement is not the same as acting mechanically
the craftsman alters his settings at every attempt
a technique that stops being practised is lost within one generation
such techniques rarely leave any written trace
goods that can be mended cost less in use than goods that are thrown away
the writer asks for fair recognition and not for idealisation
text: Too many schools still present the manual trades as a second choice, the place you land when you have failed elsewhere. That ranking deserves taking apart point by point. It ignores, first, how much thinking a skilled movement demands: fitting a part to within a fraction means reading the material without let-up, and no book stands in for that. It confuses repetition with mindless routine, when in truth the maker alters every setting each time he begins the movement again. It overlooks how easily the knowledge dies, for a technique that stops being practised is gone within one generation, leaving nothing written behind. And it rests on a false idea of worth, since goods that can be mended cost less over their life than goods thrown away. Restoring these trades is not about dressing them up, but about granting them what an honest reckoning would allow.
